passage: Himani, it's Sarita, and you're the first person I'm telling out loud. Last Tuesday I opened my phone and there was a message from a blank account: "I know your bus. Watch your back." My hands went cold. Part of me wanted to reply, to say something clever, to show I wasn't scared. But I did not. I took a screenshot of everything, blocked the account and sat there breathing. Then I walked into the kitchen and showed my father. He didn't panic. He called the school the next morning and they said we could file a report if it continued. I'm not saying it stopped my heart from racing. But I know now that this was never a game I had to win.

qa.q: What did the message on Sarita's phone say?
qa.a: It said, "I know your bus. Watch your back."

qa.q: Why did Sarita want to reply at first?
qa.a: Sarita felt scared and wanted to look brave and clever, so part of Sarita wanted to answer back. Sarita's cold hands show real fear under that wish.

qa.q: What steps did Sarita take that protected Sarita?
qa.a: Sarita did not answer, took screenshots, blocked the account and showed her father, who called the school.

qa.q: How might Sarita's father have felt seeing the message?
qa.a: He likely felt worried and protective, but he stayed calm so Sarita could feel safe telling him.

grounding: A teenager treats an online threat seriously, avoids engaging, keeps a record and reports it.

passage: I'm the neighbour who walks his dog by the lane behind Nirmala's house, and I saw a bit of this last week. A boy from her school leaned on the wall and said something low to her. I couldn't hear it, but her shoulders went stiff and she walked on without turning. Later I saw her sitting on the step with her phone, typing and saving something. I can't say what she felt, she might have been scared, or just angry, or both. The next morning she was walking to the bus with her mother, who had a folder in her hand. I mentioned what I'd seen to her mother, in case it helped. Gurpreet.

qa.q: Where did the narrator see the boy speak to Nirmala?
qa.a: He saw it in the lane behind Nirmala's house.

qa.q: What might Nirmala's stiff shoulders and silence suggest?
qa.a: They may suggest fear or anger, and Gurpreet says he cannot be certain of what she felt. Walking on without answering fits a wish to avoid engaging.

qa.q: What would you advise Nirmala to do?
qa.a: Keep a record of what was said, tell her mother, school or authorities, and avoid answering him.

qa.q: How might Nirmala's mother feel on hearing what the neighbour saw?
qa.a: She may feel worried but glad someone spoke up, since it supports the report she is making.

grounding: A teen takes an in-person threat seriously, avoids engaging, records it and tells a trusted adult, seen by an observer.

passage:
Monday: A message arrived on Pema's phone from an account with no picture: "Watch your back after school tomorrow. You'll see." Pema's hands went cold. The first urge was to type back, "Try it." Keerthana, reading over her shoulder, said, "Don't answer. Screenshot it." Pema took screenshots of the message and the account name, and showed her mother that evening. Her mother read it twice, said, "You did exactly right," and emailed the school and the class teacher before dinner.
Tuesday: The vice-principal called Pema in before first period with her mother. They listened, took copies of the screenshots, and arranged for a teacher to walk Pema to the bus. Nobody told her it was probably a joke.
Friday: The school found the account belonged to a boy in another section, and his parents were called in. Pema still checked her phone nervously, but she had stopped expecting to handle it alone.

qa.q: What did the message on Pema's phone say?
qa.a: It said, "Watch your back after school tomorrow. You'll see."

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when the message arrived, and why was the first urge risky?
qa.a: Pema felt frightened, her hands going cold, and also angry enough to want to type "Try it," which would have turned a threat into a challenge.

qa.q: Which steps kept Pema safe?
qa.a: Not replying, taking screenshots, telling her mother the same evening, and the school acting the next morning with a teacher walking her to the bus.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt reading the message over Pema's shoulder?
qa.a: Keerthana was probably worried for her friend and wanted to stop Pema from answering, which is why she said to screenshot it instead.

grounding: The before, during and after beats show a teenager treating a threat seriously, not engaging, keeping a record and reporting it to adults who act.

passage:
Zeenat, you're asking why I made such a fuss about that message on your phone? Let me tell you something from when your Pema Aunty was your age.
In my town near Darjeeling, a boy from the next school started waiting at my bus stop. One evening he stood very close and said, "If you tell anyone I'm here, you'll be sorry." I was fifteen and proud. My friends said, "Shout at him! Show him you're not scared."
I almost did. Instead I got on the bus shaking, and I told my teacher, Mrs Lepcha, the next morning, first thing. She didn't laugh. She wrote down what he'd said, the time and the place, and she walked to the bus stop with me that afternoon. The headmaster called his school.
He never came back. I didn't win anything. I just stayed safe. That's what I want for you.

qa.q: Where did the boy start waiting?
qa.a: He started waiting at Pema's bus stop.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when her friends told her to shout at him?
qa.a: She felt frightened but also proud, tempted to prove she wasn't scared, and torn between the two.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Pema Aunty's story?
qa.a: Choosing to get on the bus and tell Mrs Lepcha first thing next morning instead of shouting back; the teacher wrote it down and acted that day.

qa.q: How did Mrs Lepcha see the boy's words?
qa.a: She took them as a real threat, not a joke, which is why she recorded the details and walked Pema to the bus herself.

grounding: The elder's story shows a teenager treating an in-person threat seriously, not engaging, and reporting it to a trusted adult who keeps a record.

passage:
It was exam week, the principal was away, and the whole staff room was buried in answer sheets. On Wednesday, after Ayesha beat Ujjwal in the class monitor vote, he wrote in the class group: "Enjoy it. You'll regret this. I know which way you walk home."
A few people sent laughing faces. Someone wrote, "Reply, Ayesha! Roast him!"
Ayesha felt her heart thumping. She typed a reply, stared at it, and deleted it. Instead she screenshotted the message and the reactions, left the group, and walked straight to the staff room at lunch.
Mrs Kapoor was marking. She put the pile aside. "Show me." She read it, wrote down the time, and said, "Thank you for bringing this straight to me. It's not a joke, even in exam week." She phoned Ayesha's father and called Ujjwal's parents that afternoon. Ayesha went home by school van until it was sorted.

qa.q: Where did Ayesha go at lunch?
qa.a: She walked straight to the staff room at lunch.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when people urged her to roast Ujjwal?
qa.a: Ayesha felt scared and shaken, her heart thumping, and was tempted to reply but held back.

qa.q: Which choice of Ayesha's worked, and why?
qa.a: Deleting her reply, saving screenshots and going to a teacher the same day worked, because it treated the threat seriously and got adults to act.

qa.q: How might Mrs Kapoor have seen the message, even in a busy week?
qa.a: She saw it as a real safety issue, not a joke, so she stopped marking, recorded it, and phoned both families that afternoon.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager receiving a threat online, not engaging, keeping evidence and reporting it to a teacher who acts the same day.

passage: The message landed while Indu was waiting for the lift in her Ghaziabad apartment block: "delete ur post abt the bus stop or u will regret it. I know ur tuition time." No profile picture, an account made that day. Her thumb was already typing try me, loser, when she stopped. Her heart was hammering. This wasn't a comment war; whoever it was knew where she would be at six. She deleted the draft, took screenshots of the message and the empty profile, and went straight to Vijay Mama, who was fixing the fan in the living room. He read it twice and climbed down the ladder. "You didn't answer? Good. We don't argue with this." He called her mother, emailed the screenshots to the school principal, and that evening sat with her while they filed a complaint on the police cyber-crime portal. For the next week he walked her to tuition himself.

qa.q: What did the message say it knew?
qa.a: It said it knew her tuition time.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when her thumb started typing 'try me'?
qa.a: Indu felt scared, her heart hammering, and also angry, which pushed her toward a defiant reply; stopping shows the fear and good sense winning over the urge to fight back.

qa.q: Which steps kept Indu safer?
qa.a: She didn't reply, saved screenshots of the message and profile and told Vijay Mama at once; he informed her mother and the principal, filed a complaint that evening and walked her to tuition.

qa.q: How did Vijay Mama read the message?
qa.a: Vijay Mama took it as a real danger rather than a challenge, reading it twice and climbing straight down to act.

grounding: It shows a teenager treating an online threat seriously, not engaging, keeping a record and reporting it to a trusted adult, the school and the authorities.
